questions.question: How many abstraction layers does Simon Brown's C4 model have?
questions.explanation: C4 = Context (Level 1), Container (Level 2), Component (Level 3), Code (Level 4).

questions.question: What does 'NFRs first, technology second' mean for an architect?
options: Non-Functional Requirements (latency, availability, cost, security) drive technology choice — not the reverse
You pick the newest technology first, then measure whether it meets NFRs
NFRs are optional if the functional spec is strong
NFRs are only for the ops team, not the architect
questions.explanation: Solution architecture is derived from NFRs; choosing tech first and hoping NFRs fit is the classic anti-pattern.

questions.question: Which best distinguishes a Solution Architect from an Enterprise Architect?
options: Solution Architects only write code; Enterprise Architects only write docs
Solution Architects design a specific solution for a business problem; Enterprise Architects set org-wide standards and reference architectures
Enterprise Architects are always more senior in every organization
They are the same role with different titles
questions.explanation: SA = solution-scope depth. EA = org-scope breadth and standards. Both are architects; different altitudes.

questions.question: For a Data & Solution Architect, what does 'still hands-on' mean at 8–15 yrs?
options: Writes every line of production code themselves
Can prototype, debug, review PRs and stand up a proof-of-concept when a design needs proving out
questions.explanation: Senior architects don't own the codebase, but they can still get a PoC running to validate a design decision.

questions.question: What belongs in a C4 Level 1 (System Context) diagram, and what does NOT?
options: Internal containers, databases, and code classes
The system as a single box, plus its users and neighbouring systems — no internals
Deployment nodes and network subnets only
questions.explanation: L1 zooms all the way out: your system as one box, who uses it, what it talks to. Internals appear at L2 (Containers) and below.

questions.question: Which best describes the Inmon vs Kimball philosophy?
options: Inmon: bottom-up dimensional marts; Kimball: top-down 3NF enterprise DW
Inmon: top-down 3NF enterprise DW; Kimball: bottom-up conformed dimensional marts
questions.explanation: Inmon builds an integrated 3NF corporate DW first, then marts. Kimball builds conformed dimensional marts that add up to an enterprise view.

questions.question: In Data Vault 2.0, what does a Hub store?
options: The unique list of business keys for a concept (e.g. Customer, Product)
questions.explanation: Hub = business keys. Links = relationships. Satellites = descriptive attributes with history.

questions.question: What does SCD Type 2 do when a dimension attribute changes?
options: Overwrites the old value in place (no history)
Adds a new row with an effective date range and an is_current flag, preserving history
Deletes the row and re-inserts it
Copies the value into a separate audit table only
questions.explanation: Type 2 preserves history via a new row per change; Type 1 overwrites; Type 3 keeps prior value in a column.

questions.question: What is the 'grain' of a fact table?
options: The compression codec used for storage
The finest level of detail one row represents (e.g. one claim line per row)
questions.explanation: Grain declared explicitly ("one row = one claim line") is the single most important Kimball discipline; violating grain is the classic silent bug.

questions.question: Which scenario favors Data Vault over Kimball?
options: A small startup with one source system and simple BI
A regulated enterprise with many source systems, heavy audit needs, and frequently changing source schemas
A pure real-time streaming workload with no history
questions.explanation: Data Vault's hub-link-satellite pattern absorbs source-schema churn and preserves full auditable history — regulated multi-source environments are its home turf.

questions.question: How many layers does the Medallion architecture have?
questions.explanation: Bronze = raw, Silver = cleaned/conformed, Gold = business-ready. Some teams add a 'raw' zone before Bronze but the canonical answer is 3.

questions.question: What is Apache Iceberg's 'hidden partitioning' advantage?
options: Partition expressions are stored in table metadata so users query by natural columns and the engine prunes automatically — partitions can also evolve without rewriting data
There are no partitions at all
questions.explanation: Hidden partitioning removes the classic Hive footgun where users had to know the partition column; Iceberg lets partitioning evolve without table rewrites.

questions.question: When is a Lakehouse the wrong answer?
options: Sub-100ms OLTP transactions, sub-100ms online serving, or tiny (KB–MB) datasets
questions.explanation: Lakehouse is optimized for analytical scale on object storage. For OLTP, low-latency point lookups, or trivially small data, a purpose-built DB wins.

questions.question: What causes the 'small-files problem' on a data lake?
options: Files stored in cheap storage tiers
Many tiny files (thousands of KB-sized files per partition) forcing engines to open and read metadata for each, killing scan performance
Files being too large to fit in memory
questions.explanation: Streaming ingestion or over-partitioning creates thousands of small files; compaction (OPTIMIZE / rewrite_data_files) fixes it.

questions.question: What does an ACID open table format (Delta / Iceberg / Hudi) give a data lake that raw Parquet does not?
options: Transactional writes, schema evolution, time travel, and safe concurrent readers/writers
questions.explanation: Raw Parquet gives you files; open table formats give you a table — transactions, isolation, evolution, and time travel on top of those files.

questions.question: How many table distribution styles does Amazon Redshift support?
questions.explanation: KEY = distribute by column hash, ALL = replicate on every node (small dims), EVEN = round-robin, AUTO = Redshift picks.

questions.question: What problem does Redshift Zero-ETL solve?
options: Removes the need for a data model
Streams changes from operational sources (Aurora / RDS / DynamoDB / Kinesis) into Redshift without a customer-managed pipeline
questions.explanation: Zero-ETL is a managed CDC path — it removes the pipeline you would otherwise build with DMS or a custom Kinesis consumer.

questions.question: What does Redshift Spectrum let you query?
options: Only data physically loaded into Redshift
Data in Amazon S3 directly from Redshift, using an external schema in the Glue Data Catalog
questions.explanation: Spectrum extends Redshift SQL to S3; often used for cold data (leave it in S3) or lakehouse-style joins between Redshift-native and S3 data.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a Redshift sort key?
options: Control how data is physically ordered on disk, so range-scanned columns (like event_date) get zone-map pruning and much less I/O
questions.explanation: Sort keys drive zone maps → the query planner can skip blocks that don't match the predicate, cutting I/O dramatically for range scans.

questions.question: What does Redshift Workload Management (WLM) do?
options: Routes queries to queues with different memory + concurrency budgets, so BI dashboards and ETL don't fight each other
questions.explanation: WLM (or Auto-WLM) gives you queue-level isolation — critical when short interactive queries share a cluster with heavy ETL.

questions.question: What role does the AWS Glue Data Catalog play in a data lake?
options: Serves as the central metadata store for schemas, partitions and table definitions — shared across Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR and Glue jobs
questions.explanation: The Glue Catalog is AWS's Hive-metastore-compatible catalog — one schema definition, many engines consume it.

questions.question: Which three EMR deployment flavors does AWS offer?
options: EMR on EC2, EMR Serverless, EMR on EKS
EMR on Lambda, EMR Serverless, EMR on Fargate
EMR Studio, EMR Notebook, EMR Console
EMR Basic, EMR Standard, EMR Enterprise
questions.explanation: EMR on EC2 = classic clusters, EMR Serverless = pay-per-job Spark, EMR on EKS = share Kubernetes capacity with other workloads.

questions.question: What granularity of access control does AWS Lake Formation provide?
options: Row-, column-, and cell-level fine-grained access on tables governed by the Glue Data Catalog, plus tag-based grants (LF-tags)
No access control — it is just a UI
questions.explanation: Lake Formation adds fine-grained access on top of IAM/S3 permissions — critical for HIPAA/PII workloads.

questions.question: What is the native table format used by Amazon S3 Tables?
questions.explanation: S3 Tables are AWS-managed Iceberg tables with auto-compaction, snapshot management, and native integration with Athena / Redshift / EMR.

questions.question: When does EMR (Spark) beat AWS Glue for transformation?
options: For small ad-hoc jobs the ops team never wants to think about
For long-running, deeply-tuned Spark workloads where you need control over executor sizing, custom libraries, or non-default Spark configs — Glue's abstractions get in the way
For any workload — Glue is always slower
For any workload — EMR is always cheaper
questions.explanation: Glue is the fast-path for common transforms; EMR is chosen when you need Spark tuning depth or a specific runtime that Glue does not expose.

questions.question: What does RTO stand for, and what does it mean?
options: Rate of Throughput Optimization — target queries per second
Recovery Time Objective — the maximum acceptable time between a failure and full service restoration
Runtime Overhead — cost of observability tooling
Read Transaction Order — DB consistency guarantee
questions.explanation: RTO answers 'how long can we be down?'. Its sibling RPO (Recovery Point Objective) answers 'how much data can we lose?'.

questions.question: What is the core difference between Lambda and Kappa architectures?
options: Lambda uses AWS Lambda; Kappa does not
Lambda has separate batch and speed layers merged at query time; Kappa uses a single streaming layer for everything, replaying the stream for reprocessing
Kappa is only for machine learning
questions.explanation: Kappa argues one stream engine is simpler than maintaining two code paths; Lambda is the older two-layer design.

questions.question: How many principles / pillars does Zhamak Dehghani's Data Mesh define?
questions.explanation: The four principles: domain-oriented decentralized data ownership, data as a product, self-serve data platform, federated computational governance.

questions.question: How many pillars does the AWS Well-Architected Framework have (as of 2025)?
questions.explanation: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability. Domain-specific lenses (Data Analytics, ML) sit on top.

questions.question: When would you pick a centralized data platform over Data Mesh?
options: Always — Data Mesh is a fad
When the org has few domains (2–5 BUs), immature data-engineering culture, or strong central governance requirements — Data Mesh's federation cost outweighs its autonomy benefit at that scale
Only when the CTO says so
questions.explanation: Data Mesh's overhead (data products, federated governance) pays off at 10+ domains with mature data teams; smaller orgs usually ship faster centralized.

questions.question: What is the primary role of a Feature Store in an ML platform?
options: A governed store for engineered features, serving them consistently to both training pipelines (offline) and inference (online) — preventing training-serving skew
questions.explanation: One feature definition, two access paths (offline + online), same values — this is the whole point of a feature store.

questions.question: What causes training-serving skew?
options: Different data or feature transformations at training time vs inference time, so the model sees a distribution it was never trained on
Training on GPUs and serving on CPUs
questions.explanation: The classic cause: a Python pandas transform in the training pipeline is silently different from the SQL transform in the serving path. Feature stores solve this at the platform level.

questions.question: What are the core components of a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) architecture?
options: A retriever (vector store + embeddings), a generator (LLM), a chunking + embedding pipeline for source docs, and typically a re-ranker
A fine-tuned model and nothing else
questions.explanation: RAG grounds an LLM in retrieved context — the retrieval quality (chunking, embeddings, re-ranking) usually dominates the answer quality, not the LLM.

questions.question: When does fine-tuning beat RAG?
options: When you need the model to internalize a specific style, format, or domain vocabulary that prompt+retrieval cannot reliably enforce, and your data is stable enough to justify the training cost
When you have no training data
questions.explanation: RAG wins for freshness and factual grounding; fine-tuning wins for behavior/style/format/domain-vocab that must be baked in. Cost-latency trade-offs then decide.

questions.question: Which is a Responsible-AI guardrail worth designing into an LLM platform from day one?
options: PII detection and masking in prompts + responses, bias / drift monitoring on outputs, and a hallucination-detection eval harness in the deploy pipeline
questions.explanation: Guardrails are architectural, not decorative — they belong on the platform's critical path, not bolted on after an incident.

questions.question: In the AWS Migration 'Six R's', which one means 'keep the workload as-is on the source system for now'?
questions.explanation: The Six R's: Retire, Retain, Rehost, Replatform, Refactor, Repurchase. Retain = deliberately not migrating this workload right now.

questions.question: What is the Strangler Fig pattern in a legacy modernization?
options: Rewrite the entire legacy system in one big-bang release
Route traffic incrementally away from the legacy system to the new one, workload-by-workload, until the legacy system has nothing left to serve and can be shut down
Delete the legacy database on day one
Freeze the legacy system and never touch it again
questions.explanation: Named for a fig that grows around and eventually replaces its host tree — the new system 'strangles' the old one one route at a time.

questions.question: What does AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) do?
options: Analyzes and converts source-database schemas and SQL objects (procedures, functions, views) to a target database engine — flagging what can be auto-converted and what needs manual rewrite
questions.explanation: SCT handles the schema/code side of a heterogeneous migration (e.g. Oracle → PostgreSQL/Redshift); AWS DMS handles the data movement.

questions.question: What is the main risk of a dual-write strategy during a phased migration?
options: Two systems can silently drift out of sync if one write succeeds and the other fails, and reconciliation logic is complex to get right
It requires shutting down both systems
It only works on relational databases
questions.explanation: Dual-write requires idempotency, retry, and reconciliation — the failure modes are the hard part. Change-data-capture into a single writer is often safer.

questions.question: How many steps are in Kotter's Leading Change model?
questions.explanation: Kotter's 8 steps — create urgency, build a coalition, form a vision, communicate it, empower action, generate short-term wins, sustain acceleration, institute change.

questions.question: What is a 'walking-skeleton' architecture in an interview / capstone context?
options: The smallest end-to-end sketch that shows every layer of the system and every major decision boundary, without finishing any one component — enough to defend the design, not to build it
A skeleton diagram with no data flow
questions.explanation: Walking-skeleton captures the architecture's shape and reasoning under time pressure. Detail comes on the whiteboard during the defense.

questions.question: What three lists make up the capstone Decisions Log?
options: 3 decisions / 3 risks / 3 week-1 validation items (the 'known unknowns' made concrete)
questions.explanation: Decisions (with rejected alternative + reason), risks (with detection + mitigation), and week-1 validations (things you would go find out on the job) — a senior signal.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 2-page written Architecture Brief?
options: To give a non-panel reviewer (HR, hiring manager, week-later panelist) a prose artifact they can read in 10 minutes and compare across candidates — grades communication as well as content
questions.explanation: Prose forces reasoning to hold together — bullets hide fuzzy thinking. The brief is the HR-file artifact of the capstone.

questions.question: In the walking-skeleton discipline, what belongs on paper vs on the whiteboard vs only in the architect's head?
options: Everything on paper; nothing on the whiteboard
Decisions, NFRs and top risks on paper; the diagram and its evolution on the whiteboard; deliberate 'parked' decisions and known unknowns kept in the architect's head, ready to name if asked
Everything on the whiteboard; nothing on paper
Only tools on paper; only code on the whiteboard
questions.explanation: Architects are not stenographers; they choose what to write down and what to defend live. Naming what you deliberately did NOT decide is itself seniority signal.

questions.question: Why is the 'known unknowns' list a senior-signal in the Decisions Log?
options: It shows the candidate memorized more acronyms
It shows the candidate can articulate what they deliberately did NOT decide and why — junior architects list what they built; senior architects can name what they parked and why
It gets bonus points from HR
questions.explanation: Naming a parked decision ("I did not decide DR region until Compliance gives me the RPO") is one of the clearest signals of architect-level judgment.

questions.question: How many minutes is the executive pitch portion of the Day-10 defense?
questions.explanation: Structure: 10 min exec pitch → 15 min technical deep-dive → 15 min hostile Q&A → 5 min leadership scenario, totaling 45 min.

questions.question: How long is the hostile Q&A portion?
questions.explanation: 15 min is enough to test how the candidate handles pushback across cost, DR, scale, onboarding — the highest-signal portion of the defense.

questions.question: How long is the leadership-scenario portion at the end of the defense?
questions.explanation: 5 min at the end — one scenario ("your best engineer just quit mid-migration, what do you do?") answered concretely, not with platitudes.

questions.question: How many dimensions are in the recruitment scoring rubric used on Days 1 and 10?
questions.explanation: Data architecture, AWS solution architecture, Lakehouse/DW/Lake trade-offs, enterprise transformation, Data + AI, technical leadership, communication, cost & operational reasoning — 8 dimensions, weighted.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the seniority calibration note produced on Day 10?
options: To tell the candidate they failed

To place the candidate on a defensible ladder (Senior / Principal / Distinguished / Not-Yet-Ready), name what closes any gap, and point to where in the target org they best fit — the recruitment output the hiring committee reads
To rank all candidates against one leaderboard
questions.explanation: The note is the hiring-decision artifact: level, gap analysis, role-fit — the calibration that makes the recruitment defensible.
